title: Crispy twice-fried potato wedges
blurb: Thin wedges with a crisp potato crust and fluffy centre: simmer, lightly roughen, dry, fry, cool and fry again.
intro: The closest match to roughened roast potatoes, adapted for a deep fryer. Two trips into the oil: 130 °C, then 185 °C. The simmer is a separate cooking stage. Slender wedges give more crust per bite than whole baby potatoes. This is a source-informed home adaptation, not a kitchen-tested recipe. For a light batter shell instead, see potato wedge tempura.
equipment: Deep fryer or tall heavy pot
ingredients: to the fryer fill line, or 5 cm depth in a tall pot

mise.name: Potato wedges
mise.items: peeled; cut lengthwise, 15 mm at the thickest part

mise.name: Finishing seasoning
mise.items: salt · oregano · basil · garlic powder · pepper

steps.title: Cut slender wedges
body: Use Russet, Maris Piper, King Edward or another floury frying potato. Peel and cut lengthwise into 6 wedges per medium potato; cut a large one into 8. Aim for 15 mm at the thickest part, not a fixed number of pieces. Split any wedge wider than 20 mm. Rinse once.

steps.title: Simmer until just tender
body: Bring the water and simmering salt to a boil. Add the wedges, return to a gentle simmer, then cook about 7–10 minutes. Start checking at 6 minutes: a thin knife should enter the thickest centre easily, while the wedge still lifts intact. Tenderness decides when to drain.
steps.time: 7–10 min after returning to a simmer

steps.title: Drain, lightly roughen and dry
body: Drain thoroughly; do not rinse. Return to the empty warm pan, leave uncovered for 2 minutes, then give 2–3 gentle shakes. Stop as soon as the cut faces look lightly scuffed. Do not beat them into mash.

Spread on a rack in one layer. Let steam escape for 10 minutes, then refrigerate uncovered for about 30 minutes, until cool, firm and dry on the surface. Dryness is essential; no water droplets should remain.

steps.title: First fry; cool again
body: Use refined sunflower, rapeseed/canola or peanut oil. In an electric fryer follow its minimum and maximum fill lines. In a pot use about 5 cm depth and fill no more than one third. Fry roughly 150–200 g at a time in a 3-litre fryer, less in a small pot; wedges need room. Restore the stated temperature between batches. Surface water must be gone before any potato enters oil.
Heat oil to 130 °C. Lower dry wedges gently and fry for 5–7 minutes per batch, until a thin crust sets but the potatoes stay pale. Move carefully; the first crust is fragile.
Drain separately on the rack. Let each batch stop steaming, then chill uncovered for 20–30 minutes, until cool and firm. Complete this first fry for all batches before the final fry.

steps.title: Second fry until golden
body: Raise the oil to 185 °C. Fry the cooled wedges in small batches for about 3–5 minutes, turning gently, until golden with a rigid crisp surface. Stop at golden rather than dark brown. Drain on a rack for 30–60 seconds.

steps.title: Season and eat immediately
body: Mix the finishing salt, oregano, basil, garlic powder and pepper; crush the herbs between your fingers. Toss with the hot drained wedges, taste, then adjust the salt. Serve immediately with optional mayonnaise on the side. Keep the wedges uncovered and avoid piling them deeply.

notes: The shake roughens softened potato; it does not create new starch. Baking soda makes the cooking water alkaline and helps the outer potato break down. For more roughness, add only ⅛ tsp (about 0.6 g) ordinary baking soda to the original 2 litres of water, before the potatoes. Start checking at 4–5 minutes and shake even less. Do not use baking powder or baked baking soda. For a first batch, skip it: slender floury wedges roughen readily and are easier to handle without it.
Why these potatoes and this cut

Floury mature potatoes give the fluffy centre you want. Waxy baby potatoes stay creamier and denser. A count of six wedges only works for medium potatoes: measure the cut face. This timing is for 15 mm wedges; 10 mm pieces cook faster and 20 mm pieces need a longer simmer. Test tenderness rather than borrowing the same times.

Oregano, basil, garlic powder and pepper go on after the final fry so they keep their flavour without scorching in hot oil. Keep sauces beside the potatoes to preserve the crust. For make-ahead cooking, refrigerate the cooled first-fried wedges, covered once cold, and use within 24 hours. Uncover and check they are surface-dry before the final fry.
If the crust is soft or the wedges break

Soft or greasy crust: dry the potatoes more thoroughly, fry smaller batches and let the oil recover before each load. A hard centre means the simmer was too short; it should already be tender before frying. Broken wedges mean too much boiling, soda or shaking: reduce one of those next time. Serve uncovered on a rack rather than piling hot wedges into a bowl. If an electric fryer cannot hold 130 °C, use a tall pot and thermometer for the first fry; do not keep the same timing at an arbitrarily hotter setting.

title: Potato wedge tempura with oregano and basil
blurb: Precooked slender potato wedges in a light tempura shell, with oregano and basil added after frying. Works with packaged shrimp tempura mix.
total: ~1–1¼ h, including drying and frying in batches
intro: One trip into the oil at 175 °C, after simmering and drying the potatoes. A dry tempura mix sold for shrimp works for vegetables too: use its packet water ratio. This herb seasoning is a fusion variation. For a potato-only crust and two fries, see crispy twice-fried wedges. This is a source-informed home adaptation, not a kitchen-tested recipe.
equipment: Deep fryer or tall heavy pot
Batter bowl and larger bowl of ice
ingredients: per packet for the amount of mix shown
to the fryer fill line, or 5 cm depth in a tall pot

mise.name: Potato wedges
mise.items: peeled; cut lengthwise, 15 mm at the thickest part

steps.title: Cut and simmer the wedges
body: Use Russet, Maris Piper, King Edward or another floury frying potato. Peel and cut lengthwise into 6 wedges per medium potato; cut a large one into 8. Aim for 15 mm at the thickest part, not a fixed number of pieces. Split any wedge wider than 20 mm. Rinse once.

Bring the water and simmering salt to a boil. Add the wedges, return to a gentle simmer, then cook about 7–10 minutes. Start checking at 6 minutes: a thin knife should enter the thickest centre easily, while the wedge still lifts intact. Tenderness decides when to drain.
Do not add baking soda and do not roughen these wedges: an intact surface holds the thin batter better.

steps.title: Cool and dry thoroughly
body: Drain gently and spread apart on a rack. Let steam escape for 10 minutes, then refrigerate uncovered about 20 minutes, until cool and surface-dry. Pat away any remaining droplets. Prepare the finishing seasoning while they cool.

steps.title: Mix cold batter and coat a few wedges
body: Use refined sunflower, rapeseed/canola or peanut oil. In an electric fryer follow its minimum and maximum fill lines. In a pot use about 5 cm depth and fill no more than one third. Fry roughly 150–200 g at a time in a 3-litre fryer, less in a small pot; wedges need room. Restore the stated temperature between batches. Surface water must be gone before any potato enters oil.

Heat oil to 175 °C. Prepare 100 g dry tempura mix with ice-cold water in the packet ratio, including egg only if the packet requires it. Keep the bowl over ice, with ice outside the batter. Mix as the packet directs and use promptly; the coating should run off a spoon in a thin film.

Dust only a few dry wedges lightly with cornstarch, tap off excess, then dip in batter and let excess drip. Coat each batch immediately before frying. Do not bread with dry tempura mix or add cooked tempura crumbs to the batter.

steps.title: Fry once until the shell is crisp
body: Lower 3–5 wedges individually into the oil, without touching. In an electric fryer lower the empty basket first, then add battered wedges according to its instructions so the wet coating does not glue itself around the mesh.

Maintain 170–175 °C while frying for about 4–5 minutes, turning once, until the thin shell is crisp and pale gold and the potato is hot through. Open one thick wedge to check. Skim loose batter and restore 175 °C before the next batch. There is no second fry in this version.

steps.title: Drain, season and serve
body: Drain on a rack for 30–60 seconds. Sprinkle with the mixed salt, oregano, basil, garlic powder and pepper while hot, tasting before adding it all. Serve immediately, without covering or piling up, with optional mayonnaise on the side.

notes: Instead of the packet mix and its water, use 80 g plain flour + 20 g cornstarch + 150 ml ice-cold sparkling water. Stir briefly with a fork, leaving a few small lumps. No egg needed. Keep the separate 15 g dusting cornstarch. This is an alternative batter, not an addition to the packet mix.
Tempura mix, tempura bits or panko?

Tempura mix is uncooked powder that becomes batter with water. Tenkasu/agedama are already-fried batter bits: sprinkle a spoonful on the finished dish if you like; frying them again can burn them. Panko are breadcrumbs for a different breaded coating. If your package says shrimp tempura batter mix, use it here.
Why precook and only fry once?

A raw 15 mm wedge can stay hard inside while tempura browns. Simmering first separates those jobs: the potato becomes tender, then frying cooks the thin shell and reheats the centre. A second hot fry is useful for bare potato crust, but this thin batter shell is ready after one fry. For raw potato tempura, use a separate recipe for thin 5 mm slices.
A thin shell that sticks to the potato

Coating slips off: the potato was wet, the starch layer was too thick, or the batter was too runny. Pat the potato dry, leave only a faint starch film and let excess batter drip off. Heavy or greasy coating: keep the batter cold, avoid overmixing and restore the oil temperature between small batches. The homemade batter quantities in the note are for the original 500 g potato batch; multiply them by the same factor as the potatoes when changing servings.
sources: Idaho Potato Commission / Tiffani Faison — precooked potato tempura
